console.title: Official example replay
console.aria: Replay sky map: required and optional patches light up as exposures complete
console.explainer: This is the whole observable sky. Every mark is a patch waiting to be imaged; a filled one is done. Every 15 minutes the agent picks one to shoot — or waits for better weather.

tour.axes: The horizontal axis is right ascension — the sky's longitude — going all the way round from 0° to 360°. The vertical axis is declination, its latitude. R00–R07 across the top are the eight regions the sky is split into.
tour.tiles: Each mark is a patch to image: ◇ must be finished (REQUIRED), □ is optional (FLEXIBLE). A ring means it is high enough to shoot right now; filled in means it is already done.
tour.meridian: The dashed blue line is where the telescope is pointing right now. It drifts to the right as the Earth turns, and moves quicker around dawn, where a whole daytime is skipped.
tour.hud: The row underneath is the current slot, the weather at that moment and the progress. The four weather figures are seeing, transparency, sky brightness and instrument efficiency — hover them for an explanation. The score climbs as patches light up, and that is the number competitors are trying to maximise.

beat.interrupted: Weather cut this exposure short — it has to be redone
beat.dome_closed: Dome closed — too much cloud to observe this slot
beat.waiting: Nothing worth shooting is high enough yet; waiting for the next slot
beat.fast_forward: Fast-forwarding: the rest of this night is spent waiting
beat.night_change: Night {night} of {nights} — daytime skipped, the sky has come back round
beat.gap_short: Waiting for the next target to rise
beat.gap_nights: {n} nights with nothing worth shooting — skipping to the next exposure

console.weather_help: Seeing: how blurred stars are, lower is sharper (arcseconds). Transparency: how clear the atmosphere is, higher is better. Sky: how bright the night sky itself is. Instrument: how much the equipment is delivering right now.

vision.title: Build an open benchmark for intelligent survey operations
vision.lede: There are far more tiles than observing time, so every pointing has to be chosen.
paragraphs: Every night a survey telescope faces thousands of observable tiles. Weather changes, target visibility changes, and science priorities change. Every decision a human observer makes shapes the quality of the final cosmic sample.

We are building an open benchmark: an agent reads the state of the night sky, reasons like a seasoned observer, and decides the next observation every 900 seconds. Every participant receives the same survey plan, weather replay, inserted requests, simulator, and scoring rule, so teams differ only in strategy.

evaluation.title: Objective, public scoring rules
evaluation.lede: The scoring program is published and frozen before the competition starts and never changes afterwards. What one observation earns depends on the weather and moonlight at that moment; scheduling the right program on the right night and completing temporary observation requests on time earn extra credit, while rule violations cost points.
evaluation.formula:
total = base_science + program_bonus + request_reward
      − unsafe_observation − invalid_action − avoidable_wait
      − required_miss − flexible_shortfall − request_miss
base  = Σ_segments V_tile · (dt / t_nominal) · combined
combined = min(eff · transp · sky / (seeing · airmass), 3) · lunar

criteria.desc: Σ science_weight of the tile's targets, scaled per segment by instrument efficiency, transparency, sky quality, seeing, airmass and the lunar factor. Only completed exposures score.
+25 % / +15 % / +8 % when the chosen program matches the DARK / BRIGHT / BACKUP band of the combined quality (thresholds 0.65 and 0.40).
Temporary observation requests pay 140 per required tile when completed before the deadline and cost 190 per required tile when missed.
2000 for observing into a closed dome; 100 for an invalid action; 0.001 per second of avoidable waiting.
1000 per REQUIRED tile left unfinished, 100 per FLEXIBLE tile below the quota of four per region — applied at the end of every run, even truncated ones.
Competition weather, directional events and their forecasts are hidden. Agents run on the platform under one global wall clock and see only the published snapshots.

vision.pageSubtitle: A GOSIM Hackathon for Intelligent Survey Operations
vision.intro: This participant briefing explains why survey operations need agent observers, what a human leading observer does, how the challenge works across three planning horizons, what you submit, how scoring works, the astronomy you need, and the event schedule.

sections.title: The observing plan shapes the science sample
paragraphs: A survey telescope maps large areas of sky systematically. It does not spend a whole night on a single object; it visits thousands of tiles across many nights, building up statistically powerful samples of galaxies, quasars, and stars.

Cosmology runs on samples like these: large, uniform, well calibrated. Wide surveys reveal the large-scale structure of the universe, constrain its expansion history, underpin dark energy measurements, and tie galaxy evolution to cosmic time. Spectroscopic surveys add a third dimension — redshift. Position on the sky plus redshift gives you a three-dimensional map of cosmic structure. DESI is one concrete, public example: spectra for large samples of galaxies and quasars, used to map the expanding universe and study dark energy.

But survey operations are hard. Weather changes what a 900-second exposure is worth through seeing, transparency, and sky brightness. Target visibility shifts with airmass and position on the sky. Observing programs prefer different conditions: DARK, BRIGHT, and BACKUP. The footprint has to be covered broadly and evenly for the science to hold up. High-priority tiles, nearly finished tiles, and under-covered regions all compete for the same block of time. One bad tactical choice spends real observing time and changes every plan that follows.

Modern AI systems open a path: an assistant that reads state, calls computational tools, reasons under physical constraints, proposes a plan, monitors quality, and explains every choice. The long-term goal is an observing agent that can genuinely take part in real survey operations. This hackathon narrows that long-term vision into one focused benchmark.
sections.highlight: You build the observer’s logic. We provide the mission definition, tile table, observing constraints, weather scenarios, simulator, and evaluation protocol.

sections.title: What a human lead observer actually does
paragraphs: A seasoned lead observer makes a full set of decisions every 900-second slot: understand the science goal and decide tonight's tactical priority; read seeing, transparency, sky brightness, and the short-term forecast; judge whether tonight suits DARK, BRIGHT, or BACKUP observing; keep the tiles that are visible now, legal, and worth the time; trade off science yield, priority, airmass, footprint balance, and wasted time; finish a tile when completing it beats over-exposure; replan around weather systems, forest-fire smoke, scheduled rocket launches, and changing efficiency; use fast validation signals to calibrate later decisions; and explain why this action was chosen in this slot.

These duties are what the observing agent is taking over. We do not expect an agent to outperform a human immediately. We expect it to be evaluated objectively against a fixed interface, fixed data, and fixed scoring — so it can become a viable component of real survey operations.

sections.title: The Survey Mission Card and the challenge loop
paragraphs: Every challenge instance starts from a Survey Mission Card: the science goal, footprint area, time budget, telescope site, available observing programs, target classes, observing constraints, and scoring rules — everything a round holds you to. On this platform the mission card takes the form of published evaluation scenarios: tile catalogue, observing constraints, weather and forecasts, ad-hoc requests, simulator, and scoring configuration. The public development scenarios (dev-reference, dev-fortnight) are on the Resources page; competition scenarios are provided by the platform when the competition starts.

Every participant faces the same evaluation scenario: the overall survey plan, per-night seeing and weather replay, ad-hoc observing requests, predictable mid-term disruptions, simulator, and scoring rule are fixed. The agent receives the current state and returns the next observing action every 900 seconds.

sections.title: Plan across the survey, the week, and the next 900 seconds
paragraphs: Long term — the organizers provide the overall survey plan in the mission card, while the agent manages that plan in flight. Final scoring includes survey completeness and completion quality.

Middle term — the agent builds a flexible month, week, and day plan from progress and forecast conditions, absorbing weather systems, forest-fire smoke, scheduled launches, and newly inserted observing requests. This layer may be enabled as mission cards evolve.
Short term — every 900-second slot, the agent makes an immediate tactical choice using the middle-term plan and real-time seeing and transparency. This is the focus of the scored benchmark.

sections.title: Build a reproducibly runnable observer project
paragraphs: Any language is allowed. Submit a complete project (public repository or private ZIP) that the platform evaluates round by round in the cloud. See Docs for the interface.
The server reveals current observations step by step and scores the actual decisions. Future weather and anomaly answers remain private.
When ready, submit a complete project on Participate, then study replays to improve your strategy.
The platform keeps the full record of every evaluation — the decisions file, the run log, and a slot-by-slot replay — for organizer review, and for you to inspect why each step went the way it did.

sections.title: How scoring and the simulated environment work
paragraphs: What a completed exposure earns depends on the atmosphere and the moon at the time; matching the night's programme and answering a request add more on top. Six things cost you: unsafe observations, invalid actions, avoidable waiting, unfinished must-do patches (REQUIRED), optional shortfall per region (FLEXIBLE), and expired requests. A good agent keeps trading immediate output against coverage, weather risk, request deadlines and the time budget.

Evaluation follows open-science principles: fixed data and fixed scoring let every submitted observation result be evaluated consistently; readable result artifacts make outcomes inspectable; separate development and final-evaluation weather compare generalization instead of tuning to a known scenario.

Visualization turns completed tile fractions into an observed-target map — a 3D spatial sample and a 2D butterfly plot of sky position plus simulated redshift, in the style DESI uses — so different strategies produce visibly different maps.

The same observer interface can support future mission cards for real survey-log replay, z > 5 quasar planning, LBG planning, and target-of-opportunity inserts; the community can propose new fixed datasets for follow-up tracks.
sections.formula:
total = base_science + program_bonus + request_reward
      - unsafe_observation - invalid_action - avoidable_wait
      - required_miss - flexible_shortfall - request_miss

sections.title: A little astronomy is enough
paragraphs: You do not need an astronomy background to read the state dictionary and reason about it. A Tile is a patch of sky observed in one pointing; the Footprint is the full survey area; Targets are the object counts inside each tile. High-priority tiles carry extra scientific weight, nearly complete tiles are one exposure from completion, and under-covered regions are lagging behind the rest of the footprint.

Seeing describes atmospheric blur — lower is better. Transparency describes how clear the atmosphere is — higher is better. Sky brightness is background glow; darker is better for faint targets. Airmass measures how much atmosphere the light crosses and changes with sky position — lower is better. DARK, BRIGHT, and BACKUP are programs matched to dark, bright, and poor conditions. donefrac is tile completion: 0 means just started, 1 means finished.

The decision snapshot contains current_site_weather (observability, seeing, transparency, sky quality, instrument efficiency, active events), candidate_tiles (the legal options right now, each with geometry, airmass, lunar factor, effective weather, science value and window), active_requests, the forecasts issued so far, and progress (completed tiles, FLEXIBLE completions per region).

sections.title: Three stages from training to awards
paragraphs: The event has three stages: online training from October 2–3, online competition from October 5–7, and Awards Day at GOSIM Shenzhen on October 17.

Training covers the simulator and participant protocol; details will be announced. The competition accepts complete projects. The server reveals current information step by step and scores each complete multi-scenario batch.

about.title: The observing plan is what shapes the final science sample
about.p1: A survey telescope works by sweeping systematically across large areas of sky. Rather than spending a whole night on one object, it images thousands of patches over many nights, building a sample of galaxies, quasars and stars large enough to do statistics on.
about.p2: Modern cosmology runs on samples like that: large, uniform and well calibrated. Wide surveys reveal the large-scale structure of the universe, constrain its expansion history, underpin dark-energy measurements and tie galaxy evolution to cosmic time. Spectroscopic surveys add one more dimension — redshift. Position on the sky plus redshift is enough to map cosmic structure in three dimensions.
about.p3: DESI is a public example of this in progress: it measures spectra for large samples of galaxies and quasars to map the expanding universe and study dark energy.

hardItems.desc: Changes what a 900-second exposure is worth, through seeing, transparency, and sky brightness.
Shifts through the night with airmass and position on the sky.
Each prefers different conditions: DARK, BRIGHT, and BACKUP.
Has to be covered broadly and evenly for the science analysis to hold up.

about.hardClosing: High-priority patches, nearly finished patches and under-covered regions all compete for the same stretch of time. One bad call spends real observing time and changes the plan for the rest of the night. Decisions made at night have to work — and have to be explainable.
about.whyNowTitle: Why an observing agent, and why now
about.whyNow: The long-term goal is an observing agent that genuinely takes part in running a survey. What a human night operator does is turn science goals, weather, instrument state, completion progress and candidate patches into a decision about what to point at now. Today's AI systems make that plausible: read the state, call computational tools, reason under physical constraints, propose a plan, watch the quality, and explain every choice.
about.whyNowClosing: This hackathon narrows that long-term goal into one problem you can actually compete on.

scoring.title: How the score works
scoring.intro: What a completed exposure earns depends on the atmosphere and the moon at the time; matching the night's programme and answering a request add more. Six things cost you: unsafe observations, invalid actions, avoidable waiting, missed must-do patches, optional shortfall per region, and expired requests. A good agent trades immediate gain against covering the whole survey.

      - required_miss - flexible_shortfall - request_miss

principles.desc: Fixed data and scoring evaluate every submitted observation result under the same standard.
Readable observation-result artifacts make each team’s outcome reviewable.
Target yield, tile completion, weather response, footprint balance, and waste.
Short-term planning is primary; middle-term planning may be enabled as mission cards evolve.
Separate scenarios compare generalization instead of tuning to known weather.

scoring.principlesClosing: Future mission cards can add real survey-log replay, z > 5 quasar planning, LBG planning, and target-of-opportunity inserts. The community can propose new fixed datasets for follow-up tracks.
viz: The test data includes a deterministic table of simulated target coordinates. Each tile’s target count is bound to fixed simulated coordinates through the random seed, the tile_id, and the target class.
After a run, the simulator converts completed tile fractions into an observed-target map — how many simulated galaxies and quasars the agent actually reached.
A 3D view keeps the observed simulated universe as a spatial sample; a 2D butterfly plot folds sky position and simulated redshift together, in the style DESI uses.
Different observing strategies produce visibly different maps of cosmic structure. The visualization helps a team explain its strategy, its footprint balance, and what it missed.

items.q: I am not a strong programmer. What is the minimum?
items.a: Your agent only needs one decision function: it receives the candidates that can be observed right now, already ranked, and returns the one to observe or none to wait. See the Docs for the interface and how to submit.

items.q: Do I need an astronomy background?
items.a: Not much, though it helps. Essentially, your agent receives JSON snapshots: the current slot's weather, the candidate tiles with altitude, airmass, lunar factor, effective conditions and tile_science_value, the forecasts and requests issued so far, and your progress. The docs explain the few terms that appear. You could also team up with someone who has an astronomy background.
Yes. Create a team with a size of 1. Teams may have up to 3 members.
The formal hackathon competition allows any implementation language. Submit your complete project as a ZIP file and it runs in the cloud.

items.q: Can I use an LLM or a commercial API?
items.a: Yes, and awards require agent (LLM-driven) techniques in at least two stages. Bring your own API and quota. In Participate, either save the key encrypted on the server (used only for evaluation and verification, deleted after the hidden final results are verified) or do not save it and keep that page open during evaluations. The hidden final runs with no page open: if your program calls a model, switch to saving the key before the online phase ends.

items.q: What is the global wall clock?
items.a: Each card has one wall clock of 900 s (global_wallclock_seconds, sent in the initialize message), on Practice, in the competition and on the hidden cards. It starts at the first decision_request and covers every decision, including your think time and model calls and platform processing. There is no per-decision limit. When it expires the agent is stopped; the observations made so far still score and the terminal penalties still apply.

items.q: What is hidden on the competition scenarios?
items.a: weather.csv, weather_forecasts.csv and weather_events.csv. Your agent still sees the current slot's weather, each candidate's effective conditions (directional events applied), the forecasts issued so far and the active requests — everything the snapshots publish — but never future weather. The practice scenarios are hidden the same way.

items.q: How many submissions can I make?
items.a: Practice: 5 complete-project evaluations per team per day (separate board). Competition: 4 evaluations per team per day, each running once on every card A–D (900 s per card), and the online board keeps your best complete evaluation. Daily quotas reset at 00:00 UTC (08:00 Beijing time); failures caused by the platform are not counted. Practice ranks each scenario separately.

items.q: Is the leaderboard score the final result?
items.a: No. The online board (October 5–7) is live feedback only. After the online phase, each team's final version is evaluated once on the hidden cards E–H, and only the mean over E–H decides the final ranking; exact ties are settled by the organizers and announced with the results. Organizers verify the top teams before awards are confirmed on October 17.

items.q: Do I have to attend in Shenzhen?
items.a: No. The competition is online. Winning teams are invited to Awards Day at GOSIM Shenzhen on October 17; remote acceptance is possible.
Yes. Registration, data and scoring are free.
Not required. Before awards are confirmed, organizers may re-run top teams' final versions and ask for the complete code and the external services and models used, to reproduce the result.

items.q: What happens if my agent crashes or times out?
items.a: A run that fails to initialize within 30 seconds, exits, or answers with an invalid message ends with termination_reason agent_error or agent_initialization_error. The actions committed before that are still scored, with the terminal penalties applied, and the agent's stderr tail is shown on the submission page. If the global wall clock expires, the committed actions are scored the same way (global_wallclock_expired). Fix and resubmit within the daily limit.
Prize amounts are gross. Payment details are confirmed with winning teams after Awards Day.

items.q: Does the platform provide API credits?
items.a: The platform does not provide model credits. Cloud runs of complete projects use your own API key, set on the Participate page. Teams that complete the practice round (at least one successful practice score) each get one sponsor code, such as Kimi Coding Plan. Codes are coming soon; the captain claims it on the dashboard.

protocol.title: Protocol at a glance

desc.initialize: Sent once on stdin before the wall clock starts, no reply expected: calendar, site, the full tile and target catalogue with tile_science_value, the scoring contract and global_wallclock_seconds.
desc.decision_request: Sent once per decision: the cursor, the current slot's site weather, the candidate tiles with geometry, lunar factor and effective weather, the active requests, night and weekly publications when due, and your progress. Never any future weather.
desc.decision_response: Your agent replies with one JSON line carrying the same decision_sequence: observe a tile in a program (optionally tagged with a request_id), or wait out the slot.

protocol.truncated: Real messages from the 14-night reference run; long arrays are truncated with "… more" markers.

practice.subtitle: No astronomy background needed. If this is your first time, just do these three steps in order.
practice.s1_desc: The docs describe the task, the agent interface and scoring.
practice.s2_lead: Build your agent to the protocol in the docs.
practice.s2_desc: Iterate on the decision logic to raise your score.
s3_points: Complete project: upload your code; the platform runs and scores it in the cloud. 5 per team per day.

competition.subtitle: No astronomy background needed. Do these three steps in order to take part.
competition.s1_desc: The docs describe the task, the agent interface and scoring.
competition.s2_lead: Build your agent to the protocol in the docs.
competition.s2_desc: Iterate on the decision logic, then move to Step 3.
competition.s3_intro: Log in and open Participate: upload your code → confirm the version → start an evaluation.
s3_points: 4 evaluations per team per day; each runs your agent on the task cards A–D, 900 s per card, and the board shows the mean over A–D.
Choose your final version before the competition ends.
The final ranking uses only one evaluation of that version on the hidden cards E–H (the mean over E–H).
